::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This is the foundational case of the [Support Vector Machine](../index.qmd)
module: a **binary**, **linearly separable** problem with **two raw features**
and a **linear** decision boundary — the *hard-margin* SVM. Later notes extend it
to the soft margin (non-separable data), kernels (non-linear boundaries), and
multi-class.

I derive the classifier two ways — directly in the **weights** $\mathbf{w}$ (solved
with a quadratic-programming solver), and in terms of the **support vectors** (via
the Lagrangian and its dual). The point of doing it by hand is to build intuition
for *why* the support vectors are the only points that matter.

📄 Prefer the raw version? See my [original notes](source.qmd) — a verbatim
transcription of the handwritten derivation, mistakes and all.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Questions I worked through.** While deriving this I got stuck on a handful of
points and talked them over. Those questions turned out to be the crux of really
understanding SVMs, so I've folded them in as **"Question I had"** callouts at the
spot in the derivation where each one comes up.
:::

## Setup

Suppose we need to learn a classifier with two raw features $x_1$ and $x_2$, and
two classes labelled $y \in \{+1, -1\}$. The training data looks linearly
separable, so a straight line (a **linear** decision boundary) should do. Many
lines separate the classes; the SVM picks the one that leaves the **widest gap**
(margin $M$) between them:

```
        a    a    a          (class y = +1)
     ───────────────────      h(x) = +1   upper margin
             a  ●  ← support vector (on the margin)
     ═══════════════════      h(x) =  0   boundary
             b  ●  ← support vector (on the margin)
     ───────────────────      h(x) = -1   lower margin
        b    b    b          (class y = -1)

                     ↕  margin  M = 2 / ‖w‖  (maximized)
```

Write the linear score as

$$
h(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b,
$$

with decision boundary $h(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ and the two **margin lines**
$h(\mathbf{x}) = \pm 1$. The prediction is just the side of the boundary a point
falls on:

$$
y^* =
\begin{cases}
+1, & h(\mathbf{x}^*) > 0 \\
-1, & h(\mathbf{x}^*) \le 0.
\end{cases}
$$

## The weight vector is the normal to the boundary

A quick but useful fact: $\mathbf{w} = [w_1, w_2]^\top$ points **perpendicular** to
the decision line. Take any two points $P = (x_1^P, x_2^P)$ and $Q = (x_1^Q, x_2^Q)$
that lie *on* the boundary, so both satisfy $h = 0$:

$$
w_1 x_1^P + w_2 x_2^P + b = 0, \qquad w_1 x_1^Q + w_2 x_2^Q + b = 0.
$$

Subtracting the first from the second cancels $b$:

$$
w_1 (x_1^Q - x_1^P) + w_2 (x_2^Q - x_2^P) = 0
\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} x_1^Q - x_1^P \\ x_2^Q - x_2^P \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{v}\,=\,\overrightarrow{PQ}} = 0.
$$

The vector $\mathbf{v}$ runs *along* the boundary, and its dot product with
$\mathbf{w}$ is zero — so $\mathbf{w}$ is the **normal** to the boundary. The unit
normal is

$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\mathbf{w}}{\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert}.
$$

## Canonical form: the functional margin

Start from a symmetric band of half-width $m > 0$ around the boundary. Require
every point to sit on the correct side of its margin line:

$$
\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b \ge m \;\text{ for } y_i = +1,
\qquad
\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b \le -m \;\text{ for } y_i = -1.
$$

Both $\mathbf{w}$ and $m$ are free to scale, so we can **absorb $m$** by dividing
through: replacing $\mathbf{w}/m \to \mathbf{w}$ and $b/m \to b$ turns the right-hand
sides into $\pm 1$. This *canonical* (or *functional-margin*) normalization fixes
the scale without loss of generality:

$$
\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b \ge +1 \;\text{ for } y_i = +1,
\qquad
\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b \le -1 \;\text{ for } y_i = -1.
$$

Multiplying each case by its label $y_i$ merges the two into a single constraint:

$$
\boxed{\,y_i \big(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b\big) \ge 1\,}
\qquad i = 1, \dots, n.
$$

## The geometric margin is $2 / \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert$

Pick a point $\mathbf{x}^+$ on the $+1$ margin line and $\mathbf{x}^-$ on the $-1$
line, so $\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^+ + b = 1$ and $\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^- + b = -1$.
The margin $M$ is the length of $(\mathbf{x}^+ - \mathbf{x}^-)$ **projected onto the
unit normal**:

$$
M = \frac{(\mathbf{x}^+ - \mathbf{x}^-) \cdot \mathbf{w}}{\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert}
= \frac{(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^+) - (\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^-)}{\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert}
= \frac{(1 - b) - (-1 - b)}{\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert}
= \frac{2}{\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert}.
$$

So **maximizing the margin** $\dfrac{2}{\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert}$ is the same as
**minimizing** $\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert$, and (for a smooth, convex objective) the
same as minimizing $\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2$.

## The primal problem (weights form)

Putting the objective and the constraint together gives the **hard-margin SVM** in
its *primal* form — the one that solves directly for the weights:

$$
\underset{\mathbf{w}, b}{\text{minimize}} \;\; \frac{1}{2}\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2
\qquad \text{subject to} \qquad
y_i \big(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b\big) \ge 1, \quad i = 1, \dots, n.
$$

This is a **quadratic program**: a convex quadratic objective with linear
inequality constraints.

### Solving it with a QP solver

A generic QP solver such as `cvxopt.solvers.qp(P, q, G, h, A, b)` minimizes

$$
\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{z}^\top P\, \mathbf{z} + \mathbf{q}^\top \mathbf{z}
\qquad \text{subject to} \qquad
G \mathbf{z} \le \mathbf{h}, \;\; A \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{b}.
$$

Matching our problem, the unknown is $\mathbf{z} = [\,w_1,\, w_2,\, b\,]^\top$ and:

$$
P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0},
\quad
G = -\begin{bmatrix}
y_1 x_1^{(1)} & y_1 x_2^{(1)} & y_1 \\
y_2 x_1^{(2)} & y_2 x_2^{(2)} & y_2 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
y_n x_1^{(n)} & y_n x_2^{(n)} & y_n
\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf{h} = -\mathbf{1}.
$$

There are no equality constraints, so $A, \mathbf{b}$ are unused. The objective
$\tfrac12\mathbf{z}^\top P\mathbf{z} = \tfrac12(w_1^2 + w_2^2) = \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$
(the bias $b$ is correctly *not* penalized, which is why $P$'s last diagonal entry
is $0$). Each constraint row encodes
$y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b) \ge 1 \Leftrightarrow -y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b) \le -1$.

Solving returns $\mathbf{w}, b$ directly, and we can classify a new point with
$y^* = \operatorname{sign}\!\big([\,x_1^*\ x_2^*\,]\,\mathbf{w} + b\big)$.

## Why reformulate? Finding the support vectors

The weights form gives us a working classifier, but it does **not** tell us *which*
training points define the boundary. Those points — the ones lying exactly on the
margin lines — are the **support vectors**, and they're the whole idea behind the
method. To surface them, we rewrite the same problem in a form whose variables are
attached to the *training points* rather than to $\mathbf{w}$. That's the
**Lagrangian dual**.

::: {.callout-tip title="Question I had: what does “dual optimization problem” mean?"}
The **dual** is not a different problem — it's the *same* optimization, rewritten
so that instead of optimizing the model parameters $\mathbf{w}, b$ we optimize one
**Lagrange multiplier $\alpha_i \ge 0$ per constraint** (i.e. per training point).

| | Primal | Dual |
|---|---|---|
| Optimize over | $\mathbf{w}, b$ | $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$ |
| Objective | $\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$ | $\sum_i \alpha_i - \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j$ |
| Asks | "Where is the best boundary?" | "How much does each point matter for that boundary?" |

Once we solve for the $\alpha_i$, we recover the classifier through
$\mathbf{w} = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)}$. The points with $\alpha_i > 0$
are exactly the support vectors — that's what makes the dual worth the detour.
:::

## The Lagrangian and its stationarity conditions

Introduce a multiplier $\alpha_i \ge 0$ for each inequality constraint and fold
them into the objective. (In my handwritten notes I called these multipliers
$d_i$; the standard symbol is $\alpha_i$.)

$$
L_p(\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol{\alpha})
= \frac{1}{2}\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2
- \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i \Big[\, y_i \big(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b\big) - 1 \,\Big],
\qquad \alpha_i \ge 0.
$$

At the optimum $L_p$ is **stationary** in the primal variables. Setting the
gradients to zero:

$$
\frac{\partial L_p}{\partial \mathbf{w}} = \mathbf{w} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)} = \mathbf{0}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\boxed{\;\mathbf{w} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\;}
$$

$$
\frac{\partial L_p}{\partial b} = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\boxed{\;\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0\;}
$$

The first identity is already a headline result: **the optimal weight vector is a
linear combination of the training points**, weighted by $\alpha_i y_i$.

## From the Lagrangian to the dual

::: {.callout-tip title="Question I had: how do you get the dual from the Lagrangian?"}
The recipe is: **minimize $L_p$ over the primal variables $\mathbf{w}, b$, and
whatever is left depends only on $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$** — that's the dual function
$g(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \min_{\mathbf{w},b} L_p$. Concretely, substitute the two
stationarity results above back into $L_p$. Below I do exactly that, term by term.
:::

Substitute $\mathbf{w} = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ into the three pieces
of $L_p$.

**The squared-norm term.** Using $\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2 = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{w}$,

$$
\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2
= \left( \sum_{i} \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)} \right)^{\!\top} \left( \sum_{j} \alpha_j y_j \mathbf{x}^{(j)} \right)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j\, y_i y_j\, \big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\big)^\top \mathbf{x}^{(j)}.
$$

::: {.callout-note title="Question I had: why does ‖w‖² become a *double* sum?"}
Multiplying two sums produces a term for **every pair** of indices, so you need two
independent counters $i$ and $j$:

$$
\left( \sum_i a_i \right)\!\left( \sum_j b_j \right) = \sum_i \sum_j a_i b_j.
$$

It's the summation version of $(a_1 + a_2)(b_1 + b_2) = a_1 b_1 + a_1 b_2 + a_2 b_1 + a_2 b_2$.
Reusing one letter ($\sum_i\sum_i$) would wrongly keep only the "diagonal" pairs
$i = j$, dropping the cross terms — hence distinct $i$ and $j$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Question I had: does the transpose pass through the sum?"}
Yes — because $\alpha_i$ and $y_i$ are **scalars**, and transpose distributes over
addition and scalar multiples, $(A+B)^\top = A^\top + B^\top$ and $(cA)^\top = cA^\top$:

$$
\left( \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)} \right)^{\!\top}
= \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\big)^\top .
$$

The one caveat is **order**: for actual matrices $(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$
reverses the factors. Here every $\alpha_i y_i$ is a scalar, so there's nothing to
reorder and only the vector $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ gets transposed.
:::

**The margin term.** Substituting $\mathbf{w}$ once more (and reusing the double-sum
trick),

$$
\sum_{i} \alpha_i y_i\, \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)}
= \sum_{i} \sum_{j} \alpha_i \alpha_j\, y_i y_j\, \big(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\big)^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)}
= \sum_{i}\sum_{j} \alpha_i \alpha_j\, y_i y_j\, \big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\big)^\top \mathbf{x}^{(j)}.
$$

Note this is the **same** double sum as $\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2$.

**The bias term.** It vanishes, because $\sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0$:

$$
-\,b \sum_{i} \alpha_i y_i = 0.
$$

**Assemble.** With $S \equiv \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j (\mathbf{x}^{(i)})^\top \mathbf{x}^{(j)}$,
the norm term contributes $+\tfrac12 S$, the margin term $-S$, the constant term
$+\sum_i \alpha_i$, and the two $\tfrac12 S - S = -\tfrac12 S$ combine:

$$
g(\boldsymbol{\alpha})
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j\, y_i y_j\, \big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\big)^\top \mathbf{x}^{(j)}.
$$

## The dual problem

Everything now depends only on $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$:

$$
\boxed{\;
\underset{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\max} \;\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_i \alpha_j\, y_i y_j\, \big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\big)^\top \mathbf{x}^{(j)}
\;}
\qquad \text{s.t.} \quad \alpha_i \ge 0, \;\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i = 0.
$$

This is *also* a quadratic program, but in the $\alpha_i$. Solving it hands us the
$\alpha_i$, and hence the support vectors.

::: {.callout-important title="Question I had: shouldn’t the product be as *large* as possible, making Lₚ small?"}
This was my biggest sticking point (my handwritten notes even say "$\alpha_i$
should be as large as possible"). The catch is that the SVM Lagrangian is a
**saddle point**, not a plain minimization:

$$
\underset{\boldsymbol{\alpha} \ge 0}{\max}\;\underset{\mathbf{w}, b}{\min}\; L_p(\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol{\alpha}).
$$

We minimize over $\mathbf{w}, b$ **and** maximize over $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ — the two
act in *opposite* directions. So "increasing $\alpha_i s_i$ makes $L_p$ smaller"
is the wrong lens; for the $\alpha$-player, smaller $L_p$ is the wrong way.

And $\alpha_i$ is **not** driven to infinity, for two reasons visible in the dual
objective above:

- the $-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j \mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j$ term is a
  quadratic **penalty** that eventually dominates the linear $+\sum_i\alpha_i$ gain, so
  the maximum is finite;
- the equality constraint $\sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0$ ties the multipliers together.

What actually happens is that each constraint's *slack* decides its multiplier —
which is precisely the KKT complementary-slackness condition below.
:::

## Support vectors via KKT complementary slackness

::: {.callout-tip title="Question I had: what is the KKT condition, and why is that product zero?"}
The **Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions** are the constrained analogue of
"set the derivative to zero" — the conditions that must hold at the optimum of a
constrained problem. The key one here is **complementary slackness**:

$$
\alpha_i \Big[\, y_i \big(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b\big) - 1 \,\Big] = 0 \quad \text{for every } i.
$$

**Why must the product be zero?** Both factors are non-negative at a feasible
optimum: $\alpha_i \ge 0$ (multiplier), and the "slack"
$s_i \equiv y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b) - 1 \ge 0$ (the constraint). A
product of two non-negative numbers that the saddle point forces to zero means **at
least one factor is zero** — they can't both be positive:

- **$\alpha_i = 0$, slack $> 0$** — the point sits strictly *outside* the margin. It
  has room to spare and pulls no weight: a **non-support vector**.
- **$\alpha_i > 0$, slack $= 0$** — then $y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b) = 1$,
  i.e. the point lies *exactly on* its margin line: a **support vector**.

"Complementary slackness" is just this: either the constraint has slack, or its
multiplier is active — never both.
:::

Complementary slackness is what makes the SVM *sparse*. Every non-support vector
has $\alpha_i = 0$ and therefore drops out of $\mathbf{w} = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)}$:

$$
\mathbf{w} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)} = \sum_{i \in SV} \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)}.
$$

**The decision boundary is determined entirely by the support vectors.**

::: {.callout-tip title="Question I had: why does the weight pile onto a few support vectors instead of spreading thin over many points?"}
It feels like training could just as well hand out tiny non-zero $\alpha_i$ to
lots of points. It can't — and the reason is that spreading isn't a valid
optimum, not that the optimizer *prefers* to concentrate.

- **KKT forbids it.** Complementary slackness $\alpha_i\big[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}^{(i)}+b)-1\big]=0$
  is an on/off switch. A point strictly outside its margin has slack $s_i>0$, which
  **forces $\alpha_i=0$ exactly**. For many points to share a small $\alpha_i>0$,
  they'd *all* have to lie exactly on the margin line — which generically they
  don't. So the "thin smear" configuration violates optimality; those points get
  switched fully off. Note these are *exact* zeros, not merely small — the sparsity
  is structural (an equality condition), unlike the soft nudging of L1 penalties.
- **The boundary only feels its closest points (a quick test).** Take a point deep
  inside its own cloud and delete it, or slide it further from the boundary — the
  max-margin solution doesn't move at all. If a point can't influence
  $(\mathbf{w}, b)$, it must contribute nothing to $\mathbf{w}=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$,
  i.e. $\alpha_i=0$. Since the margin is a thin sliver, only a handful of points
  touch it.
- **A physical picture.** Think of the slab between the two margin lines inflated
  as thick as possible until it wedges against the nearest points of each class.
  Those points press back with **reaction forces** — and those forces *are* the
  $\alpha_i$. Points floating behind the front line touch nothing and push with zero
  force. This is exactly why $\mathbf{w}=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ (orientation =
  sum of contact forces) and $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$ (the two sides' forces balance).

**Soft-margin nuance:** this crisp all-or-nothing story is the hard-margin case.
With a soft margin (the `C` knob, for non-separable data), points may also sit
*inside* the margin or be misclassified, and those get $\alpha_i$ capped at $C$ —
so a few more $\alpha_i$ are non-zero, but the set is still sparse and structured
(on-margin or margin-violating points), never an even smear over the easy interior.
:::

## The classifier in support-vector form

Substituting $\mathbf{w} = \sum_{i \in SV} \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ into
$h(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^* + b$ gives the classifier written
purely in terms of the support vectors and inner products between data points:

$$
\boxed{\;
h(\mathbf{x}^*) = \sum_{i \in SV} \alpha_i y_i\, \big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\big)^\top \mathbf{x}^* + b,
\qquad
y^* = \operatorname{sign}\big(h(\mathbf{x}^*)\big).
\;}
$$

**Recovering $b$.** Pick any support vector $\mathbf{x}^{(k)}$ (where the constraint
is tight, $y_k(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}^{(k)} + b) = 1$) and solve. Using $y_k^2 = 1$:

$$
b = y_k - \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(k)} = y_k - \sum_{i \in SV} \alpha_i y_i\, \big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\big)^\top \mathbf{x}^{(k)}.
$$

(In practice one averages this over all support vectors for numerical stability.)

::: {.callout-note title="Why this form matters later"}
Notice the data enters **only through inner products** $(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})^\top\mathbf{x}^{(j)}$
— both in the dual objective and in the classifier. That's the hook for the
**kernel trick**: replace every $(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})^\top\mathbf{x}^{(j)}$ with a kernel
$K(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{x}^{(j)})$ to get non-linear boundaries for free. A
topic for a later note.
:::

## Recap: the whole chain

$$
\text{Primal} \;\to\; \text{Lagrangian } L_p \;\xrightarrow{\;\partial L_p/\partial \mathbf{w}=0,\; \partial L_p/\partial b=0\;} \text{substitute back} \;\to\; \text{Dual} \;\xrightarrow{\text{KKT}} \text{support vectors}.
$$

- **Maximize the margin** $\tfrac{2}{\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert}$ $\Leftrightarrow$ minimize
  $\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$ s.t. $y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}^{(i)}+b)\ge 1$.
- Solve the **primal** directly for $\mathbf{w}, b$ with a QP solver, **or**
- go to the **dual** to expose the support vectors: $\alpha_i > 0$ only on the margin.
- The classifier depends only on support vectors and **inner products** of data.
